newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed favors 'pro' derivs markets, exemptions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed favors 'pro' derivs markets, exemptions.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve Board believes privately negotiated derivatives deals should remain exempt from the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA), Fed governor Susan Phillips said Tuesday.

Phillips told a House Agriculture subcommittee, at its first hearing on CEA revisions, the Fed also believed sales of off-exchange derivatives to retail customers by banks and brokers "is more appropriately regulated by the federal banking regulatory agencies and the Securities and Exchange Commission, respectively."

Phillips said the Fed thought it was appropriate to re- examine rules for trading at exchanges and indicated support for so-called "professional" markets that would be limited to experienced, well-financed participants.

"In particular, the board is supportive of the development of an alternative, less intrusive regulatory regime for exchanges that limit participation to institutions and limit contracts traded to those that are not readily susceptible to manipulation -- for example, financial contracts that are settled in cash or through physical delivery of assets whose supply is highly price-elastic," she said.
Phillips is a former member of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates commodity exchanges.

The Fed did not offer suggestions on how to set up "professional" markets. But Phillips said there was a wide gap between the pilot program offered by CFTC and the structure favored by exchanges. There was "ample room for a compromise."
Under the so-called Treasury amendment to the CEA, aimed at facilitating inter-bank trading, off-exchange dealing in derivatives is exempt from CFTC control.

"In the case of privately negotiated derivative transactions between institutions, the board has supported exclusion of such transactions from the CEA in the past and continues to do so," Phillips said. "In these markets, private market discipline appears to be quite effectively and efficiently achieve the public policy objectives of the CEA."

Phillips said "it is not obvious" that CEA was the best way to oversee retail sale of derivatives. She then suggested bank regulators and the SEC oversee dealings by banks and brokers to avoid the tangle of multi-agency regulation.
